note: A starting constellation — widely-cited anchors of the field rather than a canon, and meant to be added to. These URLs were written from knowledge of the field and have NOT been verified against the live web; run `npm run check-seed` and repair anything that has moved before relying on them.

sources.title: Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
sources.summary: Twelve places to intervene in a system, ordered from the shallow (adjusting numbers) to the deep (changing the paradigm the system arises from). The foundational text for why regenerative work is rarely a technical problem.

sources.title: Shifting from 'sustainability' to regeneration
sources.summary: The paper that drew the trajectory from degenerative through neutral to regenerative practice, and argued that doing less harm is not a destination.

sources.title: Regenesis Group
sources.authors: Pamela Mang, Bill Reed, Ben Haggard
sources.summary: The practice that developed story-of-place as a working method: read the living system of a site before proposing anything, and design so the place can keep evolving.

sources.title: Circular Economy Introduction
sources.summary: The butterfly diagram and the three principles — eliminate waste, circulate materials, regenerate nature. The most-borrowed diagram in the field.

sources.title: Doughnut Economics Action Lab
sources.summary: Tools for working between the social foundation and the ecological ceiling, including the city portrait method used to downscale planetary boundaries to a place.

sources.title: Planetary Boundaries
sources.authors: Johan Rockström, Will Steffen and colleagues
sources.summary: The nine processes that regulate the stability of the Earth system, and how far past several of them we already are. The ceiling that regenerative targets are measured against.

sources.title: AskNature
sources.summary: A searchable library of biological strategies indexed by the design function they solve — how does nature manage water, resist fracture, cool itself.

sources.title: Biomimicry 3.8
sources.summary: Consultancy behind Ecological Performance Standards, which set a project's targets from what the intact local ecosystem would do on that same ground.

sources.title: Living Building Challenge
sources.summary: A certification organised as seven petals and judged on measured performance over twelve months of occupation, not on prediction.

sources.title: Cradle to Cradle Certified
sources.authors: Cradle to Cradle Products Innovation Institute
sources.summary: Product standard built on McDonough and Braungart's argument that waste is a design error — material health, circularity, clean air, water, social fairness.

sources.title: 14 Patterns of Biophilic Design
sources.authors: William Browning, Catherine Ryan, Joseph Clancy
sources.summary: Fourteen named, evidenced patterns for putting nature into buildings, each with the health outcome it is associated with.

sources.title: Carbon Leadership Forum
sources.summary: Open research and open data on embodied carbon, including the EC3 tool and the material baselines most whole-life assessments are compared against.

sources.title: RIBA 2030 Climate Challenge
sources.summary: Stepped targets to 2030 for operational energy, embodied carbon and potable water, given per square metre so projects can be held to them.

sources.title: LETI
sources.summary: Volunteer-built guidance — the Climate Emergency Design Guide and the Embodied Carbon Primer — that turned UK net-zero targets into numbers a design team can work to.

sources.title: UK Green Building Council
sources.summary: Home of the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Framework and the whole-life carbon roadmap for the sector.

sources.title: Buildings As Material Banks
sources.summary: The project that developed material passports and reversible building design — treating a building as a temporary arrangement of materials that must be recoverable.

sources.title: Circularity Gap Report
sources.summary: An annual measurement of what share of the global economy is actually circular. The number has been going the wrong way.

sources.title: Material Cultures
sources.summary: Research and practice rebuilding a construction culture around bio-based materials grown in the landscapes that surround a site — straw, hemp, timber, earth.

sources.title: Project Drawdown Solutions
sources.summary: Climate solutions ranked by modelled emissions impact, with the assumptions published — useful precisely because it lets you argue with the ranking.

sources.title: Global Footprint Network
sources.summary: Ecological footprint and biocapacity accounts by country — the source behind Earth Overshoot Day and most one-planet framings.

sources.title: One Planet Living
sources.summary: Ten principles for living within one planet's resources, developed through BedZED and used since as a masterplanning framework.

sources.title: Pattern Language and The Nature of Order
sources.summary: Alexander's argument that living structure emerges from repeated, named, locally-adapted moves — the ancestor of most attempts to write design knowledge down.

sources.title: Braiding Sweetgrass
sources.summary: Indigenous knowledge and plant science held together, and the honourable harvest as a working ethic for taking anything from a living system.

sources.title: Rewilding Britain
sources.summary: Case studies and evidence for letting land recover its own processes, at the scale where ecological function actually returns.

sources.title: New European Bauhaus
sources.summary: The EU's attempt to bind the Green Deal to beauty, sustainability and togetherness — and a live argument about whether aesthetics belong in climate policy.

sources.title: Passivhaus Trust
sources.summary: The UK body for the Passivhaus standard — fabric-first energy performance verified by measurement rather than modelled intent.

sources.title: RMI
sources.summary: Independent research on energy transition, from deep retrofit economics to embodied carbon in construction materials.

sources.title: Architects Climate Action Network
sources.summary: Organising within the profession — retrofit-first campaigning, embodied carbon regulation, and the argument for building less.
